content: The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.” These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep. [Product: Ray-Ban Meta Audio | https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/ray-ban-meta-audio/] The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware. Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you. You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.) [Image: You can see the small, customizable action button on the right-hand temple arm. I programmed it to bring up Meta AI so I don’t have to say “Hey Meta” in public. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/rayban_meta_audio_3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started. I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much. At least, not yet. Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning. [Image: Without a camera, the temple arms are much thinner, too. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/rayban_meta_audio_9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else. Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings. I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses. So what do I like about these?
